newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong 1997/98 budget seen to be "non-event".
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong 1997/98 budget seen to be "non-event".

text.p: Hong Kong's upcoming budget for the fiscal year straddling the territory's handover to China was likely to be a "non-event", said Ian Perkin, chief economist and assistant director of the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce.
But the budget for the current 1996/97 year ending on March 31 was likely to show a huge surplus far beyond the official prediction of HK$1.6 billion (US$213 million), Perkin said on Wednesday.
"The surplus will be at least HK$10 billion, and possibly as high as HK$20 billion," he told a business luncheon.
The government had underestimated its income from property transactions, continuing a long tradition that has resulted in Hong Kong's massive fiscal reserves, he said.
The territory had accumulated fiscal reserves of HK$148 billion by the end of the last fiscal year.

Perkin said Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten presented few fresh initiatives in his annual policy speech last October, which meant Financial Secretary Donald Tsang should have little fresh spending to announce in his budget speech next month.
The 1997/98 budget was also likely to be fairly tame because it straddles the British colony's handover to China at midnight of June 30, he told reporters after the luncheon.

China insisted on a say in drawing up the transitional budget. A two-year schedule to bring the Chinese participants up to speed on the budgeting process culminated in expert talks in the Joint Liaison Group (JLG), the Sino-British diplomatic body handling the handover.
British and Chinese negotiators said last week they had basically completed detailed compilation of the budget.
"I don't think there'll be very much in this budget unless there's been some momentous breakthrough in the Joint Liaison Group specialist committee," Perkin said.
"The understanding of the budget process on the Chinese side is not good enough yet to come up with anything momentous, so I don't think we'll see any major decisions made in this budget."
The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR), as the territory will be known from July 1, has been promised complete fiscal autonomy by Beijing for 50 years.
Stimulatory measures were unlikely, despite calls to keep the economy strong through the handover, Perkin said.
"I think it'll be a jawboning budget," he said. "They'll try to talk up the economy to maintain confidence, but leave all the major spending decisions...to the first budget under the SAR."

But Perkin said Hong Kong's huge surpluses could be illegal under the Basic Law, the territory's future constitution. That document not only guarantees Hong Kong's budgetary autonomy, it commits the SAR government to strive for fiscal balance.
"It will be interesting to hear what the financial secretary says about fiscal surpluses beyond July 1," he said.

The SAR government would inherit not only the fiscal reserves but the SAR Land Fund, in which half the income from government property sales has been placed. In all, it could inherit more than HK$300 billion on July 1, Perkin said.

Since the Basic Law requires Hong Kong's money to be spent in Hong Kong but does not allow current expenditures to increase at a faster rate than economic growth, that money would have to be spent on capital expenditures, he said.
"Hong Kong has a one-off opportunity to put in the infrastructure needed to make itself a true city of the 21st century," Perkin said.

More prosaically, if surpluses had to shrink, Hong Kong should lower the corporate tax rate to match the top individual rate of 15 percent, and cut stamp duty on property and share transactions, he said.
